set.body:
`modules/interaction/README.md:85-87` states it plainly: "Picking is
exhaustive and allocates geometry per target. No large-data capacity or
latency guarantee is established by these queries. Spatial indexing and
incremental updates remain separate work."

That is the blocker for hover-at-pointer on a dense scientific figure.
`PickingPlan.hits(point, tolerance)` (`Picking.scala:90-107`) and
`.nearest(point, maxDistance)` (`:109-116`) both walk every compiled target;
`PickingPlan.select(area, rule)` (`:118-134`) does the same for rectangle and
lasso brushing (`PickArea`, `:46-68`).

Ask:

- Build the index once at `Picking.compile` (`Picking.scala:136-140`) -- a
  uniform grid or R-tree over target bounds is sufficient; nothing here needs
  to be clever.
- Keep it per-facet-panel. The interaction compiler already walks
  `trained.facetPanels` (`InteractionCompiler.scala:184-187`), and a pointer
  is inside exactly one panel, so panel lookup should precede any mark
  search.
- Preserve the existing semantics exactly: `drawOrder` tie-breaking in
  `PickHit` (`Picking.scala:70`), `AreaRule.CenterInside |
  FullyContained | Intersecting` (`:26`), and tolerance in device px.
- Avoid the per-target geometry allocation on the query path; allocate at
  compile time or not at all.

Acceptance: `pick-dense` from the measurement child shows query time
independent of mark count within an order of magnitude, and every existing
picking test passes unchanged -- identical hit sets and ordering, not merely
"a hit was found".
set.title: Spatial index for picking: make hit-testing sublinear instead of an exhaustive per-target scan
